entries.test: OpenAI’s financial disclosures and credible financial reporting would establish whether it held $300 billion as of September 2025.
entries.note: Marcus quotes his own earlier assertion; the claim concerns funds then available, not eventual payment capacity.

entries.test: OpenAI’s reported cash and available funding in September 2025 would establish whether its funds were substantially below $300 billion.
entries.note: “Nowhere near” permits a plain comparison of financial scale.

entries.test: Public evaluations of GPT-5’s general capabilities and OpenAI’s statements before release would establish whether it achieved broadly human-level general intelligence and whether OpenAI suggested it would.
entries.note: “Thought (or claimed)” leaves alternatives open; the normalization commits specifically to a public suggestion.

entries.test: Oracle’s September 2025 hardware capacity, contractual computing requirements, chip procurement costs, and cash holdings would establish whether it lacked both the necessary chips and cash to purchase them.
entries.note: The assertion concerns resources held then, rather than resources Oracle might subsequently acquire.
Being astounded if payment occurs idiomatically expresses a low probability, not a firm prediction of nonpayment.

entries.test: Oracle’s historical share prices would establish its price on April 15, 2026, its September 11 price, and whether roughly $308 was the subsequent peak.
entries.note: The normalization adds that $308 was a price peak, although Marcus explicitly says the stock subsequently rose briefly.
Neither which people must agree nor what constitutes the “peak of absurdity” has a shared evidentiary test.
The line rhetorically questions his earlier superlative. The normalization adds a specific stock-market comparison drawn partly from another person’s quoted joke.
